claim: Developing Dictyostelium cells undergo highly efficient dedifferentiation, completed by most cells within 24 hr.
source: Developing Dictyostelium cells undergo highly efficient dedifferentiation, completed by most cells within 24 hr.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the RNAseq timecourse data showing gene expression returns to undifferentiated state within 24 hr (Figure 1C).

claim: Gene expression during dedifferentiation was predominantly a simple reversal of developmental changes.
source: Gene expression during dedifferentiation was predominantly a simple reversal of developmental changes, with expression changes not following this pattern primarily associated with ribosome biogenesis.
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis showing genes activated during dedifferentiation are reversed from development (Figure 1D), and quantitative analysis showing 62% of genes up-regulated during dedifferentiation were down-regulated during development.

claim: Expression changes not following the reversal pattern are primarily associated with ribosome biogenesis.
source: Gene expression during dedifferentiation was predominantly a simple reversal of developmental changes, with expression changes not following this pattern primarily associated with ribosome biogenesis.
evidence: GO analysis of genes with negative loadings to PC2 showed complete dominance by ribosome biogenesis terms (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).

claim: Mutation of genes induced early in dedifferentiation did not strongly perturb the reversal of development.
source: Mutation of genes induced early in dedifferentiation did not strongly perturb the reversal of development.
evidence: Multiple mutants tested showed wild-type or near wild-type gene expression patterns during dedifferentiation (Table 1, Figure 3A).

claim: The relative temporal ordering of cell and molecular events was not absolute during dedifferentiation.
source: This apparent robustness may arise from adaptability of cells: the relative temporal ordering of cell and molecular events was not absolute, suggesting cell programmes reach the same end using different mechanisms.
evidence: Single cell imaging showed that while most cells up-regulated act8 before division, some cells divided before act8 induction (Figure 4C), indicating temporal ordering can be reversed.

claim: Cells starting from different fates rapidly converged on a single expression trajectory during dedifferentiation.
source: In addition, although cells start from different fates, they rapidly converged on a single expression trajectory.
evidence: Single cell RNAseq showed prestalk and prespore cells, while initially separated in PC3 space, converged by around 3 hr after dedifferentiation onset (Figure 6G, H).

claim: Dedifferentiation is a critical response to tissue damage.
source: Dedifferentiation is a critical response to tissue damage, yet is not well understood, even at a basic phenomenological level.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction, with citation to Merrell and Stanger, 2016.

claim: Dedifferentiation has been implicated as a contributing process to cancer progression.
source: This reversal of developmental programmes is a widespread response to tissue damage (Merrell and Stanger, 2016), allowing replenishment of stem cell populations, and has been implicated as a contributing process to cancer progression (Friedmann-Morvinski and Verma, 2014).
evidence: Cited from Friedmann-Morvinski and Verma, 2014.

claim: Artificially triggered dedifferentiation is central to approaches to generate induced pluripotent stem cells (IPSCs) for tissue repair strategies.
source: Artificially triggered dedifferentiation is central to approaches to generate induced pluripotent stem cells (IPSCs) for tissue repair strategies (Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2016).
evidence: Cited from Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2016.

claim: Dedifferentiation is not well understood in any system.
source: Despite these important biological and clinical contexts, dedifferentiation is not well understood in any system – it would be fair to say that we do not even have an approximate conceptual framework for the main features of the process.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field presented in the introduction.

claim: c-Jun has been identified as a candidate molecular player in dedifferentiation.
source: Previous studies have identified some candidate molecular players, including c-Jun (Parkinson et al., 2008), mTORC1 (Willet et al., 2018), histidine kinases (Katoh et al., 2004) and chromatin regulators such as CAF-1 (Cheloufi et al., 2015), although these are isolated with respect to any large-scale regulatory network.
evidence: Cited from Parkinson et al., 2008.

claim: mTORC1 has been identified as a candidate molecular player in dedifferentiation.
source: Previous studies have identified some candidate molecular players, including c-Jun (Parkinson et al., 2008), mTORC1 (Willet et al., 2018), histidine kinases (Katoh et al., 2004) and chromatin regulators such as CAF-1 (Cheloufi et al., 2015), although these are isolated with respect to any large-scale regulatory network.
evidence: Cited from Willet et al., 2018.

claim: Histidine kinases have been identified as candidate molecular players in dedifferentiation.
source: Previous studies have identified some candidate molecular players, including c-Jun (Parkinson et al., 2008), mTORC1 (Willet et al., 2018), histidine kinases (Katoh et al., 2004) and chromatin regulators such as CAF-1 (Cheloufi et al., 2015), although these are isolated with respect to any large-scale regulatory network.
evidence: Cited from Katoh et al., 2004.

claim: Chromatin regulators such as CAF-1 have been identified as candidate molecular players in dedifferentiation.
source: Previous studies have identified some candidate molecular players, including c-Jun (Parkinson et al., 2008), mTORC1 (Willet et al., 2018), histidine kinases (Katoh et al., 2004) and chromatin regulators such as CAF-1 (Cheloufi et al., 2015), although these are isolated with respect to any large-scale regulatory network.
evidence: Cited from Cheloufi et al., 2015.

claim: A recurring hypothesis in IPSC studies is that dedifferentiation somehow recapitulates developmental intermediates, but in reverse.
source: A recurring feature in IPSC studies is the hypothesis that dedifferentiation somehow recapitulates developmental intermediates, but in reverse (Pasque et al., 2014; Cacchiarelli et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Pasque et al., 2014 and Cacchiarelli et al., 2015.

claim: Support for models of developmental recapitulation during dedifferentiation is based upon a few developmental markers detected within reprogramming intermediates, rather than any formal cell type classification.
source: The support for these models is based upon a few developmental markers detected within reprogramming intermediates, rather than any formal cell type classification.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the evidence supporting the recapitulation hypothesis.

claim: There is evidence for multiple gene expression trajectories during IPSC derivation.
source: The possibility of a stereotypical programme has been the subject of some debate, with some evidence for multiple gene expression trajectories, at least during IPSC derivation (Stuart et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from Stuart et al., 2019.

claim: Many characteristic models of dedifferentiation are slow, often taking days to weeks for effective return to the earlier developmental state.
source: Firstly, many of the characteristic models of dedifferentiation are slow – often taking days to weeks for effective return to the earlier developmental state.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about dedifferentiation models.

claim: IPSC generation in culture is slow, taking weeks.
source: Although IPSC generation in culture provides a more accessible model, the process is slow (weeks), a very small proportion of the starting population makes it back to the stem cell state (which means the cells one is interested in can be difficult to identify) and the process usually involves the forced expression of four transcription factors (TFs), two of which are proto-oncogenes (Karagiannis and Yamanaka, 2014).
evidence: Cited from Karagiannis and Yamanaka, 2014.

claim: A very small proportion of the starting population makes it back to the stem cell state during IPSC generation.
source: Although IPSC generation in culture provides a more accessible model, the process is slow (weeks), a very small proportion of the starting population makes it back to the stem cell state (which means the cells one is interested in can be difficult to identify) and the process usually involves the forced expression of four transcription factors (TFs), two of which are proto-oncogenes (Karagiannis and Yamanaka, 2014).
evidence: Cited from Karagiannis and Yamanaka, 2014.

claim: IPSC generation usually involves the forced expression of four transcription factors, two of which are proto-oncogenes.
source: Although IPSC generation in culture provides a more accessible model, the process is slow (weeks), a very small proportion of the starting population makes it back to the stem cell state (which means the cells one is interested in can be difficult to identify) and the process usually involves the forced expression of four transcription factors (TFs), two of which are proto-oncogenes (Karagiannis and Yamanaka, 2014).
evidence: Cited from Karagiannis and Yamanaka, 2014.

claim: Developing Dictyostelium cells can completely reverse their differentiation in around 24 hr.
source: Developing Dictyostelium cells can completely reverse their differentiation in around 24 hr (Takeuchi and Sakai, 1971; Finney et al., 1987; Katoh et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from Takeuchi and Sakai, 1971; Finney et al., 1987; Katoh et al., 2004.

claim: The normal developmental programme of Dictyostelium is induced by starvation.
source: The normal developmental programme of Dictyostelium is induced by starvation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Dictyostelium biology.

claim: Starving Dictyostelium cells aggregate together into a multicellular mound, before differentiating into two major cell types – stalk and spore.
source: Starving cells aggregate together into a multicellular mound, before differentiating into two major cell types – stalk and spore.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Dictyostelium development.

claim: Upon disaggregation and resupply of nutrients, at any time prior to terminal differentiation, Dictyostelium cells dedifferentiate, giving rise to cells that can feed, divide and develop as well as they could prior to the initial starvation process.
source: Upon disaggregation and resupply of nutrients, at any time prior to terminal differentiation, the cells dedifferentiate, giving rise to cells that can feed, divide and develop as well as they could prior to the initial starvation process.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Dictyostelium dedifferentiation.

claim: Shortly after the onset of dedifferentiation in Dictyostelium, there is evidence for a critical decision phase termed 'erasure' that corresponds to a loss of developmental memory.
source: Shortly after the onset of dedifferentiation, there is evidence for a critical decision phase. This phase – termed 'erasure' – corresponds to a loss of developmental memory (Finney et al., 1979).
evidence: Cited from Finney et al., 1979.

claim: Prior to the erasure phase, re-removal of nutrients causes rapid re-entry into the forward development process, an ability that is quickly lost as dedifferentiation proceeds.
source: Prior to this phase, re-removal of nutrients causes rapid re-entry into the forward development process, an ability that is quickly lost as dedifferentiation proceeds.
evidence: This describes the erasure phenomenon based on established knowledge.

claim: Initial microarray studies on Dictyostelium dedifferentiation implied the overall gene expression programme is distinct from development.
source: Initial microarray studies on the dedifferentiation process implied the overall gene expression programme is distinct from development (Katoh et al., 2004), going against the grain of the mammalian IPSC reprogramming studies that have argued for developmental recapitulation.
evidence: Cited from Katoh et al., 2004.

claim: The spontaneous mutant HI4 showed impairment in the loss of development-associated cell-cell adhesivity during dedifferentiation, although other features of the dedifferentiation response were unperturbed.
source: Two mutants have been shown to affect aspects of dedifferentiation: the spontaneous mutant HI4 showed impairment in the loss of development-associated cell-cell adhesivity during dedifferentiation, although other features of the dedifferentiation response were unperturbed (Finney et al., 1983).
evidence: Cited from Finney et al., 1983.

claim: Loss of the histidine kinase DhkA delayed the onset of cell population growth during dedifferentiation, although erasure, the initiation of DNA replication and overall dedifferentiation potential were not affected.
source: Loss of the histidine kinase DhkA delayed the onset of cell population growth during dedifferentiation, although erasure, the initiation of DNA replication and overall dedifferentiation potential were not affected (Katoh et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from Katoh et al., 2004.

claim: The gene expression state of dedifferentiating cells had almost completely returned to that of undifferentiated cells within 24 hr of dedifferentiation.
source: The gene expression state of the dedifferentiating cells had almost completely returned to that of undifferentiated cells within 24 hr of dedifferentiation.
evidence: Shown by PCA analysis of RNAseq timecourse data (Figure 1C).

claim: Rapid recovery of gene expression was observed whether dedifferentiation was induced using liquid (axenic) medium, or bacteria, as a food source.
source: Rapid recovery was observed whether dedifferentiation was induced using liquid (axenic) medium, or bacteria, as a food source.
evidence: Shown by PCA analysis comparing both conditions (Figure 1C).

claim: Both types of nutrition caused cells to reverse development along similar gene expression trajectories in the PCA space of the major principal components 1 and 2.
source: Both types of nutrition caused cells to reverse development along similar gene expression trajectories in the PCA space of the major principal components 1 and 2.
evidence: Shown by PCA analysis (Figure 1C).

claim: For dedifferentiation under both nutritional conditions, most of the transcriptional changes along the PC1 axis had occurred after 6 hr.
source: For dedifferentiation under both nutritional conditions, most of the transcriptional changes along the PC1 axis had occurred after 6 hr.
evidence: Shown by PCA analysis (Figure 1C).

claim: Although dedifferentiation and development trajectories had similar start and end points, they diverged from the trajectory used by cells undergoing development, primarily with respect to PC2 values.
source: Although these trajectories had similar start and end points to the corresponding developmental stages, they diverged from the trajectory used by cells undergoing development, primarily with respect to PC2 values.
evidence: Shown by PCA analysis (Figure 1C).

claim: Cells inoculated into nutrient free buffer after disaggregation showed a different path, which separated rapidly from the dedifferentiating trajectory.
source: Cells inoculated into nutrient free buffer after disaggregation showed a different path, which separated rapidly from the dedifferentiating trajectory (Figure 1C).
evidence: Shown by PCA analysis (Figure 1C).

claim: The major changes in gene expression occurring during dedifferentiation are a straightforward reversal of development.
source: Although expression trajectories during dedifferentiation and development appear distinct, consistent with earlier microarray data (Katoh et al., 2004), analysis of the genes contributing most to PC1 indicates the major changes in gene expression occurring during dedifferentiation are a straightforward reversal of development.
evidence: Shown by hierarchical clustering of genes with highest contribution to PC1 variance (Figure 1D).

claim: Gene expression milestones appear to be reached with different rates during the forward and reverse processes.
source: These gene activation processes showed a strict reversal of the gene down-regulation occurring during development, although the timing was not strictly 'mirror image', insofar as 4 hr of dedifferentiation time did not correspond to 10 hr of developmental time (Figure 1C). In other words, gene expression milestones appear to be reached with different rates during the forward and reverse processes.
evidence: Inferred from PCA analysis showing different timing relationships (Figure 1C).

claim: Cells disaggregated into non-nutrient buffer showed a strong impairment of the activations and repressions characteristic of dedifferentiation.
source: Cells disaggregated into non-nutrient buffer showed a strong impairment of the activations and repressions characteristic of dedifferentiation.
evidence: Shown by hierarchical clustering analysis (Figure 1D).

claim: Strong positive loadings to PC1 were enriched for terms related to translation and mitochondrial function.
source: Strong positive loadings to PC1 were enriched for terms related to translation and mitochondrial function (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Shown by GO enrichment analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: A large panel of ribosome proteins showed strong positive PC1 loadings, corresponding to strong expression towards the end of the dedifferentiation trajectory and at the onset of development.
source: In particular, a large panel of ribosome proteins showed strong positive PC1 loadings, corresponding to strong expression towards the end of the dedifferentiation trajectory and at the onset of development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Shown by analysis of ribosomal protein gene expression overlaid on PCA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).

claim: Strong negative loadings for PC1 were spread between processes related to terminal differentiation, cell adhesion, cAMP signalling and autophagy.
source: Strong negative loadings for PC1 were spread between processes related to terminal differentiation, cell adhesion, cAMP signalling and autophagy (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown by GO enrichment analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: From the 2428 genes up-regulated during dedifferentiation under both conditions, 62% were down-regulated during forward development.
source: Considering the portion of the trajectories with the biggest change in PC1 values, we found that from the 2428 genes up-regulated during dedifferentiation under both conditions, 62% were down-regulated during forward development.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of gene expression changes.

claim: Of the 2172 genes down-regulated during dedifferentiation under both conditions, 60% were up-regulated during development.
source: Similarly, of the 2172 genes down-regulated during dedifferentiation under both conditions, 60% were up-regulated during development.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of gene expression changes.

claim: There is a strong symmetry between the dedifferentiation and development trajectories, with most genes showing changes (above a two fold threshold) directly reversing their behaviour between the two processes.
source: These data suggest a strong symmetry between the dedifferentiation and development trajectories, with most genes showing changes (above a two fold threshold) directly reversing their behaviour between the two processes.
evidence: Inferred from the quantitative overlap analysis showing 60-62% reversal.

claim: The csaA gene is strongly reactivated immediately after the induction of dedifferentiation.
source: A more specific example of developmental reversal is suggested by the strong reactivation of the csaA gene immediately after the induction of dedifferentiation (Figure 2D).
evidence: Shown by RNAseq read counts over time (Figure 2D).

claim: The csaA gene is normally expressed when cells aggregate during development, before the transcript declines in the aggregate, and encodes a cell surface protein to facilitate cell adhesion during development.
source: The gene is normally expressed when cells aggregate during development, before the transcript declines in the aggregate, and encodes a cell surface protein to facilitate cell adhesion during development.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about csaA function.

claim: Other well-characterised aggregation-specific genes such as carA and pldB show similar dynamic behaviour to csaA during dedifferentiation.
source: We also identified other well-characterised aggregation-specific genes showing similar dynamic behaviour, such as carA and pldB.
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of the RNAseq data.

claim: For dedifferentiation in bacteria, there is a 41% overlap between early dedifferentiation genes and aggregation-specific genes.
source: For dedifferentiation in bacteria, we found a 41% overlap (165/402 genes) between the dedifferentiation and aggregation genes.
evidence: Quantitative analysis comparing gene sets.

claim: The 41% overlap between dedifferentiation and aggregation genes in bacteria-based dedifferentiation implies a strong enrichment of aggregation markers in the early dedifferentiation gene set.
source: This overlap was compared to a simulated scenario with 402 genes sampled at random (10,000 times) from the entire genome. In the simulations, the median overlap between the dedifferentiation genes and the randomly sampled genes was found to be only 22%, with the 41% value never observed. This implies a strong enrichment of aggregation markers in the early dedifferentiation gene set.
evidence: Statistical comparison to random sampling simulation.

claim: Liquid medium cultures showed only 15% overlap between dedifferentiation and aggregation-induced genes.
source: However, this effect was specific to the bacteria-based dedifferentiation, with liquid medium cultures showing an effect in the opposite direction, with only 15% overlap between dedifferentiation and aggregation-induced genes.
evidence: Quantitative analysis comparing gene sets.

claim: The re-induction phenomenon of aggregation genes is not consistently a feature of dedifferentiation trajectories.
source: We conclude that the re-induction phenomenon is not consistently a feature of dedifferentiation trajectories.
evidence: Inferred from the different behavior in bacteria vs. liquid medium conditions.

claim: Genes such as csaA and carA may be repressed by strong cAMP signalling in the mound, and if this signalling is relieved by disaggregation then the repressive influence on transcription is removed, triggering re-induction.
source: An alternative explanation is that genes such as csaA and carA are repressed by strong cAMP signalling in the mound (Van Haastert et al., 1992; Masaki et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2014; Corrigan and Chubb, 2014). If this signalling is relieved (by disaggregation) then the repressive influence on transcription is removed, triggering re-induction.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on cited literature about cAMP signaling.

claim: Dedifferentiation is characterised by several distinctive classes of gene expression, occurring at different phases during the process.
source: Dedifferentiation is characterised by several distinctive classes of gene expression, occurring at different phases during the process (summarised in Figure 2E).
evidence: Revealed by hierarchical clustering of RNAseq data (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).

claim: Early 'off' events correspond to the down-regulation of genes encoding fruiting body components, in addition to other developmentally induced genes.
source: Early 'off' events (Figure 2—figure supplement 6) correspond to the down-regulation of genes encoding fruiting body components, in addition to other developmentally induced genes.
evidence: Shown by hierarchical clustering and GO analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).

claim: Following the initial early 'off' step are a series of transient inductions starting with genes for protein degradation, then cytoskeletal components and regulators, before widespread induction of ribosome and mitochondrial biogenesis.
source: Following this initial step are a series of transient inductions (Figure 2—figure supplement 7) starting with genes for protein degradation, then cytoskeletal components and regulators, before widespread induction of ribosome and mitochondrial biogenesis.
evidence: Shown by hierarchical clustering and GO analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).

claim: After the transients come the stable long-term induction of translation and mitochondrial respiration components.
source: After the transients come the stable long-term induction of translation and mitochondrial respiration components (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Shown by hierarchical clustering and GO analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).

claim: Cell cycle genes are expressed initially during dedifferentiation (reflecting their role in development) before switching off, then re-inducing as dedifferentiation proceeds.
source: A final grouping includes cell cycle genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 9), which are expressed initially (reflecting their role in development; Muramoto and Chubb, 2008) before switching off, then re-inducing as dedifferentiation proceeds.
evidence: Shown by hierarchical clustering and GO analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 9), with citation to Muramoto and Chubb, 2008.

claim: None of the mutants in six transcription factors showing rapid induction in their expression during early dedifferentiation showed clear changes in gene expression compared to wild type.
source: To determine the genes regulated by these TFs, we mutated the coding sequences of their genes, then carried out RNAseq on the mutants during dedifferentiation. To our surprise, none of the mutants showed clear changes in gene expression compared to wild type (Table 1, examples shown in Figure 3A).
evidence: Shown by RNAseq analysis of mutants (Table 1, Figure 3A).

claim: None of eight mutants enriched from an insertional mutagenesis screen for delayed induction of act8-mNeonGreen were consistently impaired in their ability to induce mNeonGreen during dedifferentiation.
source: As an attempted proof of concept, we regenerated eight of the enriched mutants by homologous recombination in the act8-mNeonGreen cells. Unexpectedly, none of these mutants were consistently impaired in their ability to induce mNeonGreen during dedifferentiation (Table 1).
evidence: Shown by flow cytometry analysis of mutants (Table 1).

claim: PCNA expression was induced with relatively normal timing in forG- cells.
source: PCNA expression was induced with relatively normal timing in forG- cells (Figure 3B), however induction of a longer transcript was impaired.
evidence: Shown by Northern blot analysis (Figure 3B).

claim: Clonal recovery on bacterial lawns of dedifferentiating forG- cells was reproducibly lower than that for wild types.
source: Clonal recovery on bacterial lawns of dedifferentiating forG- cells was reproducibly lower than that for wild types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), perhaps due to the strong phagocytosis defect of the mutants.
evidence: Shown by clonal recovery assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Despite the slightly perturbed induction of PCNA and weakened clonal survival, other markers of dedifferentiation timing, such as the hspE and rpl15 genes, showed normal induction in forG- cells.
source: Despite the slightly perturbed induction of PCNA and weakened clonal survival, other markers of dedifferentiation timing, such as the hspE and rpl15 genes, showed normal induction (Figure 3B, left panels).
evidence: Shown by Northern blot analysis (Figure 3B).

claim: At the whole transcriptome level, the forG- cells showed a slight delay in the dedifferentiation response, although the starting position of the mutants in the PCA space was slightly shifted with respect to wild type.
source: At the whole transcriptome level, the forG- cells showed a slight delay in the dedifferentiation response, although the starting position of the mutants in the PCA space was slightly shifted with respect to wild type (Figure 3C).
evidence: Shown by PCA analysis of RNAseq data (Figure 3C).

claim: The rasS- mutants showed a weakened induction of PCNA, however the induction of hspE and rpl15 was similar to wild type.
source: As with the forG- cells, the rasS- mutants showed a weakened induction of PCNA, however the induction of hspE and rpl15 was again similar to wild type, suggesting no genome-wide impairment of gene expression (Figure 3B, right panels).
evidence: Shown by Northern blot analysis (Figure 3B).

claim: Dedifferentiating rasS- cells showed no defect in clonal recovery on bacterial lawns.
source: Unlike the forG- cells, dedifferentiating rasS- cells showed no defect in clonal recovery on bacterial lawns (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), implying no absolute requirement for RasS in dedifferentiation.
evidence: Shown by clonal recovery assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Defects in dedifferentiation gene expression can be detected in mutants with strong growth defects, however the gene expression dynamics still appear relatively robust.
source: These observations indicate that defects in dedifferentiation gene expression can be detected in mutants with strong growth defects, however the gene expression dynamics still appear relatively robust.
evidence: Inferred from the analysis of forG- and rasS- mutants.

claim: Both the forG- and rasS- mutants have defects in macropinocytosis, which impair their growth in liquid medium.
source: Both the forG- and rasS- mutants have defects in macropinocytosis, which impair their growth in liquid medium.
evidence: This is stated based on known phenotypes of these mutants.

claim: Even after 30 hr of dedifferentiation, when cell division is widespread in the culture and gene expression has returned to the undifferentiated state, the wild-type fluid uptake was only half the normal level of undifferentiated Dictyostelium cells.
source: Even after 30 hr of dedifferentiation, when cell division is widespread in the culture and gene expression has returned to the undifferentiated state, the wild-type fluid uptake was only half the normal level of undifferentiated Dictyostelium cells.
evidence: Shown by fluid uptake measurements (Figure 3D).

claim: A small but reproducible increase in fluid uptake could be detected around 8 hr into dedifferentiation.
source: However, a small but reproducible increase in fluid uptake could be detected around 8 hr into dedifferentiation (Figure 3D).
evidence: Shown by fluid uptake measurements (Figure 3D).

claim: The modest amount of macropinocytosis during the early phase of dedifferentiation suggests the process is not strongly required for most of the gene expression changes occurring early on.
source: This modest amount of macropinocytosis during the early phase of dedifferentiation suggests the process is not strongly required for most of the gene expression changes occurring early on, and might explain why mutants with strong defects in fluid uptake do reasonably well in activating dedifferentiation gene expression.
evidence: Inferred from the fluid uptake data and mutant phenotypes.

claim: Processes other than macropinocytosis drive the response to nutrition during dedifferentiation.
source: These observations hint that processes other than macropinocytosis drive the response to nutrition.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that gene expression changes occur before substantial macropinocytosis.

claim: Standard sensors of the nutritional state of the cell show rapid responses to the induction of dedifferentiation.
source: In line with this possibility, standard sensors of the nutritional state of the cell (Jaiswal and Kimmel, 2019) show rapid responses to the induction of dedifferentiation (Figure 3E), with cells showing rapid loss of the phosphorylated form of AMPKα and rapid induction in the phosphorylation of the mTORC1 substrate 4E-BP1, long before macropinocytosis could be detected.
evidence: Shown by phospho-western blotting (Figure 3E), with citation to Jaiswal and Kimmel, 2019.

claim: Cells show rapid loss of the phosphorylated form of AMPKα during early dedifferentiation.
source: In line with this possibility, standard sensors of the nutritional state of the cell (Jaiswal and Kimmel, 2019) show rapid responses to the induction of dedifferentiation (Figure 3E), with cells showing rapid loss of the phosphorylated form of AMPKα and rapid induction in the phosphorylation of the mTORC1 substrate 4E-BP1, long before macropinocytosis could be detected.
evidence: Shown by phospho-western blotting (Figure 3E).

claim: Cells show rapid induction in the phosphorylation of the mTORC1 substrate 4E-BP1 during early dedifferentiation.
source: In line with this possibility, standard sensors of the nutritional state of the cell (Jaiswal and Kimmel, 2019) show rapid responses to the induction of dedifferentiation (Figure 3E), with cells showing rapid loss of the phosphorylated form of AMPKα and rapid induction in the phosphorylation of the mTORC1 substrate 4E-BP1, long before macropinocytosis could be detected.
evidence: Shown by phospho-western blotting (Figure 3E).

claim: The first mitosis appeared considerably delayed compared to the onset of cell-cycle gene expression.
source: The first mitosis appeared considerably delayed compared to the onset of cell-cycle gene expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown by comparison of single cell imaging data with RNAseq timecourse (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The median time of mitotic onset was 17.9 hr after dedifferentiation onset.
source: The median time of mitotic onset was 17.9 hr after dedifferentiation onset, contrasting the 5–6 hr at which cell cycle gene expression reached a plateau (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: Shown by single cell imaging data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The division time corresponds to the stage at which the transcriptional changes of dedifferentiation are essentially complete.
source: More striking is that the division time corresponds to the stage at which the transcriptional changes of dedifferentiation are essentially complete (Figure 1C).
evidence: Inferred by comparing division timing to PCA trajectory completion.

claim: A considerable amount of post-transcriptional information processing is required before the first division can be activated during dedifferentiation.
source: These data suggest a considerable amount of post-transcriptional information processing is required before the first division can be activated, and indicates that division is not required for the majority of the transcript changes of dedifferentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the delay between gene expression changes and division.

claim: Division is not required for the majority of the transcript changes of dedifferentiation.
source: These data suggest a considerable amount of post-transcriptional information processing is required before the first division can be activated, and indicates that division is not required for the majority of the transcript changes of dedifferentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that most transcriptional changes occur before division.

claim: After the first mitotic division, the overall duration of the second cell cycle (median 7.4 hr) was more similar to the undifferentiated cycle time (6.1 hr).
source: After the first mitotic division, the overall duration of the second cell cycle (median 7.4 hr) was more similar to the undifferentiated cycle time (6.1 hr) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggestive of a near-complete return to the undifferentiated state, more in line with the gene expression time course data.
evidence: Shown by single cell imaging data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Dedifferentiating cells displayed considerable heterogeneity in both division time and act8 induction profile.
source: Dedifferentiating cells displayed considerable heterogeneity in both division time and act8 induction profile (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,C,D).
evidence: Shown by single cell imaging data (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: The bulk behaviour of act8 induction indicated dividing cells induced expression more rapidly than non-dividing cells.
source: The bulk behaviour of act8 induction indicated dividing cells induced expression more rapidly than non-dividing cells (Figure 4B) and in line with this, the overwhelming majority (Figure 4C) of dividing cells up-regulated act8 before the first division.
evidence: Shown by single cell imaging data (Figure 4B, C).

claim: The overwhelming majority of dividing cells up-regulated act8 before the first division.
source: The bulk behaviour of act8 induction indicated dividing cells induced expression more rapidly than non-dividing cells (Figure 4B) and in line with this, the overwhelming majority (Figure 4C) of dividing cells up-regulated act8 before the first division.
evidence: Shown by single cell imaging data (Figure 4C).

claim: The timing of the first mitosis was strongly correlated to the time of onset of act8 induction.
source: The timing of the first mitosis was strongly correlated to the time of onset of act8 induction (Figure 4E).
evidence: Shown by single cell imaging data (Figure 4E).

claim: The rate of act8 induction was higher in dividing cells than in those that did not divide.
source: The rate of act8 induction did not show a strong correlation with timing of the first mitosis across replicate experiments (r = −0.229, mean of four experiments), however the rate of act8 induction was higher in dividing cells than in those that did not divide (Figure 4F).
evidence: Shown by single cell imaging data (Figure 4F).

claim: There is a strong degree of temporal coupling between the first mitosis and the onset of gene expression characteristic of the undifferentiated state.
source: Overall, these data suggest a strong degree of temporal coupling between the first mitosis and the onset of gene expression characteristic of the undifferentiated state, however the ordering of events is not absolute and the tendency of cells to carry out both processes either slow or fast is probably indicative of an overarching feature of cell state dictating dedifferentiation rate, rather than a strict sequence of events.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation analysis and observation of variable ordering.

claim: The ordering of events between mitosis and gene expression is not absolute during dedifferentiation.
source: Overall, these data suggest a strong degree of temporal coupling between the first mitosis and the onset of gene expression characteristic of the undifferentiated state, however the ordering of events is not absolute and the tendency of cells to carry out both processes either slow or fast is probably indicative of an overarching feature of cell state dictating dedifferentiation rate, rather than a strict sequence of events.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that some cells divide before act8 induction.

claim: The tendency of cells to carry out both processes either slow or fast is probably indicative of an overarching feature of cell state dictating dedifferentiation rate, rather than a strict sequence of events.
source: Overall, these data suggest a strong degree of temporal coupling between the first mitosis and the onset of gene expression characteristic of the undifferentiated state, however the ordering of events is not absolute and the tendency of cells to carry out both processes either slow or fast is probably indicative of an overarching feature of cell state dictating dedifferentiation rate, rather than a strict sequence of events.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between act8 induction timing and division timing.

claim: As cells become aggregation competent, they initially increase their motility, until aggregation, when their motile behaviour becomes more suited to migration within a 3D tissue, and so cells show reduced motility on surfaces.
source: Another developmentally regulated property of cells is motility (Varnum et al., 1986). As cells become aggregation competent, they initially increase their motility, until aggregation, when their motile behaviour becomes more suited to migration within a 3D tissue, and so cells show reduced motility on surfaces.
evidence: Cited from Varnum et al., 1986.

claim: Cell motility reverses during dedifferentiation, with cells increasing their speed over the first few hours, before slowing transiently, then becoming more motile again as dedifferentiation proceeds.
source: This tendency reverses during dedifferentiation, with cells increasing their speed over the first few hours, before slowing transiently, then becoming more motile again as dedifferentiation proceeds (Figure 5A).
evidence: Shown by single cell tracking data (Figure 5A).

claim: Dedifferentiating cells showed considerable heterogeneity in their motility, with speed profiles falling into two clusters.
source: Dedifferentiating cells showed considerable heterogeneity in their motility, with speed profiles falling into two clusters (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Shown by clustering analysis of single cell tracking data (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: The majority (around 70%) of cells showed very little motility during dedifferentiation.
source: The majority (around 70%) of cells showed very little motility, whereas a small subpopulation showed a strong increase in migration, in line with the population average behaviour.
evidence: Shown by clustering analysis of single cell tracking data (Figure 5B).

claim: A small subpopulation of cells showed a strong increase in migration during dedifferentiation, in line with the population average behaviour.
source: The majority (around 70%) of cells showed very little motility, whereas a small subpopulation showed a strong increase in migration, in line with the population average behaviour.
evidence: Shown by clustering analysis of single cell tracking data (Figure 5B).

claim: Persistence was similar between the two motility clusters.
source: Persistence was similar between the two clusters (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Shown by analysis of single cell tracking data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The motile population showed little tendency to divide during the 25 hr movie.
source: Monitoring the subsequent first mitoses of these cells revealed the motile population showed little tendency to divide during the 25 hr movie (Figure 5C).
evidence: Shown by single cell imaging data (Figure 5C).

claim: Most slow moving cells divided by the end of image capture.
source: In contrast, most slow moving cells divided by the end of image capture.
evidence: Shown by single cell imaging data (Figure 5C).

claim: The heterogeneity in motile behaviour during dedifferentiation might be consistent with some kind of bet-hedging response, with cells effectively speculating on staying put and proliferating, versus spreading in search of new habitats.
source: These observations of heterogeneity in the behaviour of cells reveal a slow moving dividing population and more rapid moving population that has deferred cell division. This might be consistent with some kind of bet-hedging response, with cells effectively speculating on staying put and proliferating, versus spreading in search of new habitats, reminiscent of heterogeneous motile behaviour in Bacillus and other bacteria (Henrichsen, 1972).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the motility heterogeneity, with analogy to bacterial behavior cited from Henrichsen, 1972.

claim: The starting expression level of CryS during dedifferentiation was not related to whether or not a cell divided during the 28 hr of image capture.
source: The starting expression level of CryS during dedifferentiation was not related to whether or not a cell divided during the 28 hr of image capture (Figure 6A), and the division time was uncorrelated to CryS level (Figure 6B).
evidence: Shown by single cell imaging data (Figure 6A, B).

claim: The division time was uncorrelated to CryS level.
source: The starting expression level of CryS during dedifferentiation was not related to whether or not a cell divided during the 28 hr of image capture (Figure 6A), and the division time was uncorrelated to CryS level (Figure 6B).
evidence: Shown by single cell imaging data (Figure 6B).

claim: The motility of cells was not clearly linked to their CryS expression level.
source: Finally, the motility of cells was not clearly linked to their CryS expression level (Figure 6C), with no significant differences between the cell speed distributions of the 20% cells with highest CryS expression and the remainder of the population (KS test: p=0.46 and 0.22 for two replicates).
evidence: Shown by single cell imaging data (Figure 6C).

claim: The cell heterogeneity in motility and division time occurring during dedifferentiation arises independently of starting cell fate.
source: We conclude that the cell heterogeneity in motility and division time occurring during dedifferentiation arises independently of starting cell fate.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of correlation between CryS expression and division/motility.

claim: The data show two major clusters in single cell RNAseq, with the right cluster enriched for genes induced in the multicellular stage of development.
source: An overview of the data, showing the first two principal components, is shown in Figure 6D (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1 for the replicate). The data show two major clusters, with the right cluster enriched for genes induced in the multicellular stage of development.
evidence: Shown by PCA analysis of single cell RNAseq data (Figure 6D).

claim: The left cluster of cells (negative PC1 values) shows a clear gradient of expression of genes repressed during development, such as ribosomal components.
source: Conversely, the left cluster of cells (negative PC1 values) shows a clear gradient of expression of genes repressed during development, such as ribosomal components.
evidence: Shown by PCA analysis of single cell RNAseq data (Figure 6D).

claim: PC1 reflects developmental time, with positive values corresponding to cells early in dedifferentiation, and negative values corresponding to cells closer to the undifferentiated state.
source: Comparing these data to the population transcriptomics data presented earlier implies PC1 reflects developmental time, with positive values corresponding to cells early in dedifferentiation, and negative values corresponding to cells closer to the undifferentiated state (Figure 6E).
evidence: Inferred by comparing single cell and population RNAseq data.

claim: There was no clear evidence in PC1-PC2 space for multiple trajectories during dedifferentiation.
source: There was no clear evidence in this PCA space for multiple trajectories.
evidence: Shown by PCA analysis of single cell RNAseq data (Figure 6D).

claim: Stalk and spore fates showed clear separation in PC1-PC3 space.
source: Stalk and spore fates showed clear separation in PC1-PC3 space (Figure 6G).
evidence: Shown by PCA analysis of single cell RNAseq data (Figure 6G).

claim: The set of prespore markers highlights different cells to the prestalk markers.
source: The set of prespore markers highlights different cells to the prestalk markers.
evidence: Shown by overlaying marker expression on PCA (Figure 6G).

claim: Using PC1 as a proxy for developmental time, prespore markers rapidly switch off, whilst the prestalk expression persists in cells with negative PC1 values.
source: Using PC1 as a proxy for developmental time, prespore markers rapidly switch off, whilst the prestalk expression persists in cells with negative PC1 values.
evidence: Shown by overlaying marker expression on PCA (Figure 6G).

claim: The differing behaviours of prestalk and prespore cells during dedifferentiation do not interfere with the convergence of cell states.
source: The differing behaviours of prestalk and prespore cells during dedifferentiation do not interfere with the convergence of cell states (Figure 6H).
evidence: Shown by PCA analysis of single cell RNAseq data (Figure 6H).

claim: The beginning of trajectory merging is around 3 hr after dedifferentiation onset.
source: By corroboration with Northern blot data of the csaA gene (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E), we find that the beginning of trajectory merging is around 3 hr after dedifferentiation onset.
evidence: Inferred by comparing single cell RNAseq with Northern blot timing (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).

claim: The later time points (3–6 hr) are relatively bunched, whereas the earlier time points are scattered in single cell RNAseq PCA space.
source: The later time points (3–6 hr) are relatively bunched, whereas the earlier time points are scattered.
evidence: Shown by PCA analysis of single cell RNAseq data (Figure 6G, H).

claim: Most transcriptional changes occur early during dedifferentiation.
source: This implies, as suggested earlier, that most transcriptional changes occur early during dedifferentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the bunching of later timepoints in PCA space.

claim: The timescale of convergence during dedifferentiation is similar to that measured for the cell fate separation process during forward developmental progression.
source: Notably, the timescale of convergence is similar to that measured for the cell fate separation process during forward developmental progression (Antolović et al., 2019), implying no strong resistance to cell state change that is specific to dedifferentiation.
evidence: Comparison to published data cited from Antolović et al., 2019.

claim: There is no strong resistance to cell state change that is specific to dedifferentiation.
source: Notably, the timescale of convergence is similar to that measured for the cell fate separation process during forward developmental progression (Antolović et al., 2019), implying no strong resistance to cell state change that is specific to dedifferentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the similar timescales of convergence and divergence.

claim: The dedifferentiation response of Dictyostelium cells is remarkable in its speed and reliability when compared to mammalian dedifferentiation contexts.
source: When compared to mammalian dedifferentiation contexts, the dedifferentiation response of Dictyostelium cells is remarkable in its speed and reliability, with most cells reversing their development in around 24 hr, whilst retaining their ability to generate a full complement of cell fates upon re-induction of development.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion.

claim: Most Dictyostelium cells reverse their development in around 24 hr whilst retaining their ability to generate a full complement of cell fates upon re-induction of development.
source: When compared to mammalian dedifferentiation contexts, the dedifferentiation response of Dictyostelium cells is remarkable in its speed and reliability, with most cells reversing their development in around 24 hr, whilst retaining their ability to generate a full complement of cell fates upon re-induction of development.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Dictyostelium dedifferentiation.

claim: The forward and reverse trajectories are not strict mirror image processes, with differences in the relative timing of events, and key transcriptional differences, notably a strong induction of ribosomal biogenesis components as cells return to the undifferentiated state.
source: The forward and reverse trajectories are not strict mirror image processes, with differences in the relative timing of events, and key transcriptional differences, notably a strong induction of ribosomal biogenesis components as cells return to the undifferentiated state.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the RNAseq analysis.

claim: Cells from both fates appear to converge on the same gene expression trajectory rapidly during dedifferentiation, with no clear difference in the dedifferentiation phenotypes of spore and stalk-directed cells.
source: Cells from both fates appear to converge on the same gene expression trajectory rapidly during dedifferentiation, with no clear difference in the dedifferentiation phenotypes of spore and stalk-directed cells.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the single cell RNAseq analysis.

claim: The gene expression programme of dedifferentiation is robust to mutation of genes induced early in the programme, with relatively normal gene expression in mutants otherwise displaying strong proliferation defects.
source: The gene expression programme of dedifferentiation is robust to mutation of genes induced early in the programme, with relatively normal gene expression in mutants otherwise displaying strong proliferation defects.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the mutant analysis.

claim: The efficiency and apparent robustness of dedifferentiation may be related aspects of the dedifferentiation response.
source: The efficiency and apparent robustness may be related aspects of the dedifferentiation response.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation in the discussion.

claim: Dedifferentiation is induced experimentally by disaggregation of cells, followed by a nutritional stimulus.
source: Dedifferentiation is induced experimentally by disaggregation of cells, followed by a nutritional stimulus.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Disaggregation means a loss of stimuli related to cell contacts and dilution of other signals, such as cAMP.
source: Disaggregation means a loss of stimuli related to cell contacts and dilution of other signals, such as cAMP.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what disaggregation does to the cells.

claim: The nutritional stimulus, whether the peptone-based medium or bacteria, is a complex mix of food biomolecules, likely to enter the cellular metabolic network via many pathways.
source: The nutritional stimulus, whether the peptone-based medium or bacteria (the more natural food source), is a complex mix of food biomolecules, likely to enter the cellular metabolic network via many pathways.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the nature of the nutritional stimulus.

claim: Given the obvious complexity of the overall stimulus to dedifferentiate, it may be unlikely that the cell, regardless of its fate tendency, has any real choice but to efficiently obey this overwhelming sensory input.
source: Given the obvious complexity of the overall stimulus to dedifferentiate, it may be unlikely that the cell, regardless of its fate tendency, has any real choice but to efficiently obey this overwhelming sensory input, and that perturbation of any single molecule will be insufficient to substantially arrest the process.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why dedifferentiation is robust.

claim: Perturbation of any single molecule will be insufficient to substantially arrest the dedifferentiation process.
source: Given the obvious complexity of the overall stimulus to dedifferentiate, it may be unlikely that the cell, regardless of its fate tendency, has any real choice but to efficiently obey this overwhelming sensory input, and that perturbation of any single molecule will be insufficient to substantially arrest the process.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why single mutants don't block dedifferentiation.

claim: Although different events during differentiation (gene expression and mitosis) show a distinct temporal sequence, at the single cell level the temporal ordering can be reversed.
source: Along these lines, although we observed that different events during differentiation (gene expression and mitosis) show a distinct temporal sequence, at the single cell level the temporal ordering can be reversed.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from single cell imaging.

claim: Cell programmes can unfold in different ways to the same stimulus, potentially contributing to robustness.
source: This implies that cell programmes can unfold in different ways to the same stimulus, potentially contributing to robustness.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the variable temporal ordering.

claim: The lack of a rigid dependency between temporal phases of dedifferentiation may explain why mutants may have some impairment in individual aspects of reversing development, whilst leaving the majority of dedifferentiation responses unperturbed.
source: This lack of a rigid dependency between temporal phases of dedifferentiation may also explain why mutants may have some impairment in individual aspects of reversing development, whilst leaving the majority of dedifferentiation responses unperturbed (Finney et al., 1983; Katoh et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the temporal flexibility to mutant phenotypes, with citations to Finney et al., 1983 and Katoh et al., 2004.

claim: The dhkA mutants undergo erasure, replicate their DNA with normal timing and show wild-type levels of clonal recovery following dedifferentiation.
source: Despite this phenotype, as with our growth-defective mutants, other features of the dhkA mutant dedifferentiation response are normal. The dhkA mutants undergo erasure, replicate their DNA with normal timing and, based on plating efficiency of finger-stage cells, show wild-type levels of clonal recovery following dedifferentiation.
evidence: This is stated based on published data about dhkA mutants.

claim: The dhkA phenotype aligns well with the mutants described in this study (forG and rasS) that dedifferentiate fairly effectively despite an underlying cell health problem.
source: Overall, these observations suggest the dhkA phenotype aligns well with the mutants described in our study (forG and rasS) that dedifferentiate fairly effectively despite an underlying cell health problem.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing dhkA to the mutants studied here.

claim: The re-expression of markers from an early developmental time during dedifferentiation was anecdotal, based on well-known genes, and did not stand up strongly to a more formal analysis.
source: In Dictyostelium, we also identified the re-expression of markers from an early developmental time, in line with the mammalian literature, however the evidence was anecdotal, based on well-known genes, and did not stand up strongly to a more formal analysis.
evidence: This is a summary of findings regarding aggregation gene re-induction.

claim: The apparent lack of a coherent developmental intermediate during dedifferentiation in Dictyostelium may to a certain extent underlie the speed and efficiency of developmental reversal.
source: The apparent lack of such a coherent developmental intermediate during dedifferentiation in Dictyostelium may to a certain extent underlie the speed and efficiency of developmental reversal.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: The differences between dedifferentiation in Dictyostelium and during IPSC generation appear to be systemic.
source: The differences between dedifferentiation in Dictyostelium and during IPSC generation appear to be systemic, and it seems unlikely at the present time that we could use knowledge from the former to improve the latter.
evidence: This is an assessment in the discussion.

claim: The efficiency of dedifferentiation in Dictyostelium may ultimately come down to the likelihood that it is a physiological response, whereas the generation of IPSCs is clearly not.
source: The efficiency of dedifferentiation in Dictyostelium may ultimately come down to the likelihood that it is a physiological response, whereas the generation of IPSCs is clearly not.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: In the migratory slug phase of development many cells fall out of the rear of the slug onto the substrate, where they are then able to re-enter the feeding part of the lifecycle, if bacteria are present, and then fully re-differentiate once the supply of bacteria is exhausted.
source: In the migratory slug phase of development many cells fall out of the rear of the slug onto the substrate, where they are then able to re-enter the feeding part of the lifecycle, if bacteria are present, and then fully re-differentiate once the supply of bacteria is exhausted (Kuzdzal-Fick et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from Kuzdzal-Fick et al., 2007.

claim: The falling out of cells from the slug rear is in effect a dispersal strategy, bet-hedging against the potential for a proliferative disadvantage occurring within the dormant spore state.
source: This is in effect a dispersal strategy, bet-hedging against the potential for a proliferative disadvantage occurring within the dormant spore state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the biological function of the slug rear cell behavior.

claim: Meaningful parallels between the dedifferentiation responses of Dictyostelium and mammalian cells seem more likely in situations where mammalian cells dedifferentiate as part of the normal course of events, such as during responses to tissue damage and metabolic stress.
source: Meaningful parallels between the dedifferentiation responses of Dictyostelium and mammalian cells seem more likely in situations where mammalian cells dedifferentiate as part of the normal course of events, such as during responses to tissue damage and metabolic stress.
evidence: This is a speculative assessment of where the findings might be most relevant.
